source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics, 17th ed. self-assessment sets. Answer keys are the source's own; explanations carry current-practice notes where the original key has been superseded.

quizzes.topicMix: Derm 3, EM 3, Gen 3, ID 11, Metab 7, N-acquired 3, N-cutaneous 3, N-epilepsy 4, N-infection 1, N-malform 3, N-neuromusc 1, Resp 4, Rheum 4

questions.stem: A mother removes a small tick from her 5-yr-old's neck in an endemic area; duration of attachment unknown. Next step?

options.text: Reassure and order serology in 1 mo
Reassure and instruct her to call if a rash develops at the site

questions.explanation: Risk after a single bite is very small; most infected patients develop erythema migrans even without a remembered bite. (Current IDSA guidance permits single-dose doxycycline when the tick is an engorged Ixodes attached over 36 hr in a highly endemic area.)

questions.stem: Features of tyrosinemia type I include all except:
questions.explanation: Fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase deficiency; succinylacetone accumulation causes porphyria-like neurologic crises and renal tubulopathy; HCC in about 40% untreated. Nitisinone (NTBC) plus diet has transformed prognosis. Cataracts are galactosemia, not tyrosinemia.

questions.stem: Erythema nodosum is associated with all of the following except:
questions.explanation: Associated with GAS, TB, Yersinia, histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis, IBD, SLE, JRA, sarcoidosis, sulfonamides, phenytoin, OCPs.

questions.stem: A 12-yr-old with confirmed CF has 8 days of intermittent diffuse cramping abdominal pain unrelated to meals, no guarding, no emesis or diarrhea. Cause?
questions.explanation: Impacted stool (meconium ileus equivalent) from insufficient pancreatic enzyme replacement; consider fibrosing colonopathy if on high-dose enzymes.

questions.stem: Sodium valproate is chosen for a 12-yr-old. Which factor markedly increases the risk of fatal hepatic necrosis?
questions.explanation: Risk is highest under age 2, with polytherapy, and with underlying metabolic disease (POLG mutations are a contraindication). Pancreatitis is the other idiosyncratic toxicity.

questions.stem: A 4-yr-old after submersion arrives comatose, GCS 4, pH 7.12, PaCO2 35, PaO2 145, normal vitals. Which finding most likely predicts a favorable outcome?
questions.explanation: Clinical improvement within 6-24 hr is the best predictor; no lab or imaging test has predictive power. Management is supportive: normal oxygenation and blood pressure, no hyperventilation, no dextrose loading.

questions.stem: A 10-day-old term infant treated with phototherapy for hyperbilirubinemia develops an annular, scaly, erythematous eruption on the forehead; KOH is negative. His mother has intermittent joint pain. Most appropriate next step?
questions.explanation: Neonatal lupus: transplacental IgG (anti-Ro/La) causes rash (often UV-provoked), cytopenias, hepatitis, and heart block; all resolve except the block. Only 1 in 10 has both rash and ECG changes, so serology is the diagnostic step; ECG is also reasonable.

questions.stem: Patients with Turner syndrome should have their chromosomes examined for Y material because they may:
questions.explanation: Y material is present in 5-10%; gonadoblastoma risk warrants prophylactic gonadectomy.

questions.stem: Parents of a newborn with myelomeningocele ask about hydrocephalus. Best description of the risk?

options.text: Related to the cause of the malformation

questions.explanation: Hydrocephalus, from the associated Chiari II malformation, develops in most; head ultrasound or CT at birth and serial head circumference.

questions.stem: NF1 is defined by six or more cafe-au-lait macules (over 5 mm prepubertal, 15 mm postpubertal) plus at least one of the following except:

options.text: Two neurofibromas or one plexiform neurofibroma

questions.explanation: Ash-leaf hypomelanotic macules are tuberous sclerosis (present in over 90%). Lisch nodules are present in the vast majority of NF1 patients after age 12. (Revised 2021 criteria add heterozygous pathogenic NF1 variant and choroidal abnormalities.)

questions.stem: A 3-yr-old with cyanotic congenital heart disease has 2 wk of fever, bifrontal headache, lethargy, and vomiting, then a 10-min focal seizure, papilledema, and right hemiparesis with hyperreflexia. Cause of the hemiparesis?
questions.explanation: Right-to-left shunt bypasses pulmonary filtration; other predisposing conditions are chronic otitis and sinusitis, endocarditis, and immunodeficiency. Ring-enhancing lesion on imaging; LP is contraindicated.

questions.stem: Which finding excludes a diagnosis of infant botulism?

options.text: No ingestion of honey or corn syrup

questions.explanation: Bulbar palsy (weak suck, feeble cry, drooling, ptosis, sluggish pupils) precedes descending symmetric weakness; constipation is early but soft stools do not exclude it; reflexes are preserved early. Most cases have no honey exposure (environmental spores). Confirm by toxin or organism in stool; EMG shows brief small-amplitude potentials with incremental response to rapid repetitive stimulation (presynaptic).

questions.stem: Most common sequela of bacterial meningitis?
questions.explanation: Sensorineural hearing loss, potentially attenuated by dexamethasone (best evidence for Hib); audiology before discharge. Seizures occur in 20-50% acutely (cytokines, fever) but chronic epilepsy is unusual.

questions.stem: In a developing country a 2-yr-old has fever, dysphagia, lethargy, and a gray-brown leather-like adherent membrane over the posterior oropharynx and hypopharynx. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Adherent membrane extending beyond the faucial area, relatively little fever, and dysphagia distinguish diphtheria from streptococcal and EBV pharyngitis.

questions.stem: A child with homocystinuria (cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency) is started on high-dose pyridoxine without response. Most likely explanation?
questions.explanation: Folate must be replete for a pyridoxine trial to be interpretable; about half of patients are B6-responsive. Nonresponders need methionine restriction and betaine.

questions.stem: A 4-yr-old girl has 3 days of low-grade fever, crampy abdominal pain with emesis, swollen knees, and lower-extremity petechial rash. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Abdominal pain, vasculitic rash, arthritis, nephritis with normal platelets; GI involvement may progress to intussusception. A preoperative UA showing hematuria and proteinuria in a child labeled "acute abdomen" should cancel the operation pending evaluation. Coronary aneurysm is not an HSP complication (Kawasaki).

questions.stem: A 2-yr-old improving from a URI develops high fever, brassy cough, toxic appearance, and retractions; can lie flat, no drooling or dysphagia, clear lungs. Most appropriate antibiotic?
questions.explanation: Bacterial tracheitis, most often S. aureus (current practice adds MRSA coverage).

questions.stem: A 4-yr-old boy has a first unprovoked 10-min generalized tonic-clonic seizure with normal exam an hour later. Most appropriate management?
questions.explanation: EEG stratifies recurrence risk and identifies a syndrome; treatment is not started after a single unprovoked seizure with normal exam. MRI is reserved for focal features, abnormal exam, or focal EEG.

questions.stem: A febrile infant does not smile, has a dull expressionless face, and is not alert to social overtures. Management?

options.text: 20 mL/kg saline and reassess in 1 hr
IM ceftriaxone after blood culture, return in the morning
Blood, urine, and CSF cultures, ceftriaxone, admit
If over 6 mo, blood culture and return if still febrile

questions.explanation: Response to social stimuli is a critical observation; this 3-mo-old had pneumococcal meningitis.

questions.stem: Hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia is associated with all except:

options.text: Partial or complete absence of sweat glands

questions.explanation: Hypotrichosis is the rule. Inability to sweat causes recurrent high fevers, so it belongs in the FUO differential.

questions.stem: Trinucleotide repeats are implicated in all of the following except:
questions.explanation: NF1 is caused by heterogeneous loss-of-function variants (about half de novo). Repeat disorders show anticipation; Friedreich ataxia (GAA intronic, recessive) is the exception to dominant inheritance.

questions.stem: To prevent myelomeningocele, folic acid supplementation must begin:
questions.explanation: The neural tube closes by day 28, before most pregnancies are recognized. 0.4 mg daily for all women of childbearing potential; 4 mg for a prior affected pregnancy, which also lowers recurrence.

questions.stem: A previously healthy 1-yr-old presents with afebrile seizures; skin exam shows confetti-like white spots on the right leg that the parents call a birthmark. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Hypomelanotic macules (ash-leaf or confetti) are the earliest sign; use a Wood lamp. TSC1/TSC2, mTOR pathway; cortical tubers, subependymal nodules, SEGA, cardiac rhabdomyomas, renal angiomyolipomas; vigabatrin for infantile spasms, mTOR inhibitors for SEGA.

questions.stem: A 10-yr-old girl has new school problems, obsessive-compulsive behavior, and occasional uncontrolled hand movements; no medications. Evaluation is most likely to reveal:
questions.explanation: Poststreptococcal OCD and chorea (Sydenham spectrum; the PANDAS construct remains contested).

questions.stem: A 16-yr-old girl has abrupt high fever, vomiting, diarrhea, diffuse sunburn-like rash, pharyngeal and conjunctival hyperemia, oliguria, and postural hypotension. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Kawasaki is uncommon after age 5, less severe, and not associated with hypotension or diarrhea.

questions.stem: An 18-yr-old has menstrual-associated abdominal pain out of proportion, alternating constipation and diarrhea, and during an episode hypertension, tachycardia, urinary retention, and port-wine urine. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: HMBS deficiency, autosomal dominant with low penetrance; rare before puberty; precipitated by drugs (barbiturates, sulfonamides), fasting, stress, and menses. No photosensitivity. Urine PBG during the attack; treat with hemin and glucose.

questions.stem: An 18-yr-old has swollen right wrist and left ankle, bilateral Achilles tenderness, and limited forward bending 2 wk after antibiotic treatment of urethral discharge. Most appropriate agent?
questions.explanation: Reactive arthritis needs only symptomatic NSAID therapy. Triggers: Shigella, Salmonella, Yersinia, Campylobacter, Cryptosporidium, Giardia, Chlamydia.

questions.stem: A 4-yr-old with 4 days of URI, fever 40.1, SpO2 88%, splinting, dullness and decreased breath sounds over the right posterior chest, WBC 30,000, opacified right hemithorax with layering fluid on decubitus film. Next step?
questions.explanation: Symptomatic parapneumonic effusion; both diagnostic and therapeutic.

questions.stem: Landau-Kleffner syndrome is characterized by all except:
questions.explanation: More common in boys. Acquired epileptic aphasia (verbal auditory agnosia) with sleep-activated spikes (often electrical status in slow sleep); valproate, steroids, or benzodiazepines; GRIN2A in a subset.

questions.stem: A 15-yr-old pedestrian struck by a car is alert with pulse 140, RR 40, BP 70/50, distinct heart sounds, decreased left breath sounds. Next step?

options.text: Needle thoracentesis of the left hemithorax

questions.explanation: Symptomatic hemo/pneumothorax with shock is evacuated before imaging.

questions.stem: A 2-mo-old former 32-wk infant has a rapidly growing hemangioma involving the perioral region, chin, and anterior neck; parents wonder about asthma. Next step?
questions.explanation: Beard-distribution hemangioma may herald a subglottic hemangioma that can obstruct the airway. (Propranolol is now standard therapy.)

questions.stem: A disease affecting all daughters but no sons of an affected father, and 50% of sons and daughters of an affected mother, is most likely:
questions.explanation: Absence of male-to-male transmission with all daughters affected is the signature. Examples: X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets, incontinentia pigmenti (male-lethal), Rett syndrome (MECP2, mostly de novo).

questions.stem: A 6-mo-old with a tuft of thick black hair over the sacrum since birth and no symptoms. Next step?
questions.explanation: Sacral hair tufts, hemangiomas, dimples above the gluteal cleft, and lipomas mark occult dysraphism (tethered cord). Ultrasound suffices before ossification of the posterior elements (under about 3 mo); MRI thereafter.

questions.stem: A neonate has a facial port-wine stain in the V1 distribution and focal seizures. What is the leptomeningeal angioma of Sturge-Weber thought to represent?

options.text: A primitive venous plexus that failed to regress

questions.explanation: Somatic activating GNAQ mutation; ipsilateral parieto-occipital leptomeningeal angioma with tram-track calcification, contralateral hemiparesis, and glaucoma. Aspirin and early seizure control are used to limit stroke-like episodes.

questions.stem: Physical features of Sydenham chorea include all except:
questions.explanation: Hypotonia is the rule. A major Jones criterion; latency of months after streptococcal pharyngitis so ASO may be normal; penicillin prophylaxis and echocardiography.

questions.stem: A springtime community outbreak of fever, mild rash, and arthralgia; a woman in late pregnancy recovers, then delivers a stillborn infant with hydrops fetalis. Etiology?
questions.explanation: B19 infects erythroid precursors, producing fetal anemia and nonimmune hydrops; intrauterine transfusion can be curative.

questions.stem: A 2-mo-old has failure to thrive, emesis, alopecia, rash, and chronic metabolic acidosis; an older sibling died at 3 mo with hypotonia and lactic acidosis. Important diagnostic study?
questions.explanation: Biotinidase (or holocarboxylase synthetase) deficiency impairs the four biotin-dependent carboxylases; ketoacidosis, hyperammonemia, seizures, hearing loss, optic atrophy, dermatitis, and alopecia. Oral biotin is curative; on newborn screen.

questions.stem: All of the following about Kawasaki disease are true except:

options.text: Asian children have the highest risk
Exposure to an affected patient greatly increases risk
It is the leading cause of acquired heart disease in US children

questions.explanation: Outbreaks occur but person-to-person transmission is uncommon.

questions.stem: Most common bronchial foreign body?
questions.explanation: A persistent or worsening focal consolidation after apparent recovery warrants bronchoscopy.

questions.stem: Characteristics of simple partial (focal aware) seizures include all except:
questions.explanation: Awareness is retained; some patients converse during the event.

questions.stem: A 12-yr-old has a nail puncture wound of the foot; last tetanus immunization documented at age 4. Recommended?
questions.explanation: Completed primary series plus a contaminated wound with more than 5 yr since last booster. (Tdap is now preferred for the adolescent booster.)

questions.stem: A 6-day-old breast-fed infant has poor feeding, vomiting, jaundice, hepatomegaly, bruising, elevated transaminases, prolonged clotting, and aminoaciduria; urine reducing substances are negative. Most appropriate next step?
questions.explanation: Reducing substances can be negative if lactose intake has been curtailed; enzyme assay is definitive (invalid after transfusion). Classic galactosemia predisposes to E. coli sepsis and cataracts; on newborn screen.

questions.stem: A 2-mo-old has conjunctivitis, tachypnea, mild cough, no fever, and bilateral crackles. Agent?
questions.explanation: Insidious afebrile staccato cough with crackles and without wheeze distinguishes it from RSV; treat with oral erythromycin 14 days (topical therapy of the conjunctivitis does not prevent pneumonia).

questions.stem: At 1 yr a child has new spasticity, head circumference above the 95th percentile, and diffuse white matter disease on MRI. Most relevant test?
questions.explanation: Canavan disease (aspartoacylase, ASPA; autosomal recessive, Ashkenazi founder alleles); NAA elevated in urine, blood, and on MR spectroscopy. Macrocephalic leukodystrophy with optic atrophy; Alexander disease is the other macrocephalic leukodystrophy (frontal predominance, GFAP).

questions.stem: A 9-day-old presents with fever, lethargy, and poor feeding; sepsis evaluation including CSF is unremarkable and ampicillin and cefotaxime are begun. Two days later cultures are negative but she deteriorates with hypotension, depressed consciousness, thrombocytopenia, and elevated transaminases. Indicated change?
questions.explanation: Disseminated neonatal HSV: hepatitis, coagulopathy, and shock with negative bacterial cultures. Localized SEM and disseminated disease present at a mean of 5-6 days; CNS disease at 8-12 days.

questions.stem: A 5-mo-old with gross motor delay, hypotonia, macroglossia, cardiomegaly, and CK 860 has a short P-R interval on ECG. Most helpful diagnostic study?
questions.explanation: Pompe disease (GSD II, lysosomal acid maltase); the short PR with massive LVH distinguishes it from SMA. Vacuolar myopathy on biopsy; enzyme assay on dried blood spot is now the first-line test, and alglucosidase alfa ERT changed a uniformly fatal infantile course. On newborn screen in many states.

questions.stem: A 6-wk-old has proven pertussis. Mother has had a bad cough for 2 wk, father is well, and three fully immunized asymptomatic siblings (20 mo, 6 yr, 8 yr) live at home. Besides the infant, who should receive erythromycin?
questions.explanation: Macrolide prophylaxis for all household and close contacts regardless of age, immunization status, or symptoms. (Azithromycin is now preferred, especially in young infants.)

questions.stem: A 10-yr-old in New Jersey has an 8-cm annular erythematous rash on the back and unilateral peripheral facial palsy. Neck is supple. Next step?
questions.explanation: Facial palsy is relatively common in pediatric Lyme disease and may be the only manifestation; it usually resolves in 2-8 wk whether or not treated. Serology is unnecessary with erythema migrans; LP is reserved for meningeal signs.

questions.stem: Rate of vertical HIV transmission without antiretroviral treatment?
questions.explanation: US and European cohorts; higher in Africa and Haiti. Prenatal, intrapartum, and 6-wk neonatal zidovudine cut transmission to 3-4% (now under 1% with suppressive maternal ART).

questions.stem: Recommended treatment of cervical lymphadenitis due to nontuberculous mycobacteria?
questions.explanation: Antimycobacterial therapy only if M. tuberculosis cannot be excluded or chronic drainage develops. Lymphadenitis is the most common NTM disease in children.

questions.stem: Which serologic set is most consistent with acute primary EBV infection?

options.text: IgM-VCA negative, IgG-VCA 1:160, EA 1:40, EBNA negative
IgM-VCA negative, IgG-VCA negative, EA 1:40, EBNA negative

questions.explanation: IgM-VCA is the best single test for acute infection; anti-EBNA appears 3-4 mo after infection and its presence argues against acute disease.

questions.stem: A 7-mo-old boy has weakness, cardiomyopathy, and hypoketotic hypoglycemia with fasting; an older sister has episodic muscle pain and rhabdomyolysis; both have hypoketotic dicarboxylic aciduria. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: VLCAD (originally described as LCAD) involves skeletal and cardiac muscle; SCAD does not produce hypoketotic hypoglycemia.

questions.stem: A positive ANA (1:80 or greater) is associated with all of the following except:
questions.explanation: A positive ANA is a nonspecific marker of increased lymphocyte activity in many inflammatory states.

questions.stem: A 9-yr-old with vomiting and diarrhea has systolic BP 75. You should:

options.text: Give 20 mL/kg lactated Ringer in D5W

questions.explanation: Minimum normal systolic for age 1-10 is 70 + 2 x age, here 88. Isotonic crystalloid without dextrose.

questions.stem: A 15-mo-old has a 10-min generalized seizure with T 40 C. Which history most increases the risk of future seizures?
questions.explanation: Risk of later epilepsy rises with family history of epilepsy, preexisting neurodevelopmental abnormality, and complex features (focal, prolonged, recurrent within 24 hr). About 30% recur with future fevers; that recurrence is predicted by young age, low-grade fever, brief fever-to-seizure interval, and family history of febrile seizures.

questions.stem: Most helpful finding to differentiate croup from epiglottitis?
questions.explanation: (source key). Epiglottitis in the unimmunized: high fever, toxicity, air hunger, drooling, without barking cough. (Drooling is the more commonly taught discriminator; the source keys the cough.)

questions.stem: Stevens-Johnson syndrome (erythema multiforme major) is associated with all except:

options.text: Involvement of two or more mucous membranes

questions.explanation: No agreed indication for systemic steroids; management is burn-unit style supportive care, withdrawal of the culprit drug, and topical ophthalmic steroids to limit scarring. Secondary bacterial infection and sepsis are the main threats; antibiotics are for proven or strongly suspected infection.

questions.stem: Tay-Sachs disease is best described as:
questions.explanation: Autosomal recessive HEXA deficiency; the common Ashkenazi allele is a 4-bp insertion (frameshift), the French Canadian allele a large deletion. Late-onset and juvenile forms exist as well.

questions.stem: Ptosis, progressive external ophthalmoplegia, pigmentary retinopathy, heart block, and proximal myopathy in a teenager. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Single large-scale mtDNA deletion (usually sporadic); onset before 20, ragged red fibers, elevated CSF protein, cerebellar ataxia, hearing loss, endocrinopathy. Conduction block is the lethal complication and warrants a pacemaker.

questions.stem: A 5-yr-old has 6 mo of increasing gait difficulty and urinary incontinence; exam shows hyperreflexia, clonus, and bilateral Babinski signs in the legs, absent reflexes in the arms, and symmetric 3/5 weakness in all limbs. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Lower motor neuron signs at the cervical level with upper motor neuron signs below localize to the cervical cord; bladder involvement and progression demand urgent MRI.

questions.stem: A 6-mo-old girl is strongly left-handed and delayed in sitting and in using the right hand; MRI shows a large porencephalic cyst in the left MCA territory. Most likely to establish the cause?
questions.explanation: Early handedness is pathologic. Perinatal arterial stroke is often multifactorial, but prothrombotic evaluation (factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A, protein C and S, antithrombin, antiphospholipid antibodies, lipoprotein(a)) is standard.

questions.stem: A 1-yr-old has ascending paralysis with intact cranial nerves; CSF is normal except for elevated protein. Likely precipitating infection?
questions.explanation: Guillain-Barre: albuminocytologic dissociation, areflexia, symmetric ascending weakness, prolonged F waves early; IVIG. Campylobacter (also CMV, EBV, Mycoplasma) is the classic antecedent; ganglioside molecular mimicry.

questions.stem: Most useful test for the diagnosis of neurocysticercosis?
questions.explanation: Solitary cyst with or without enhancement, or a scolex; the leading cause of acquired epilepsy worldwide. Albendazole plus steroids for viable parenchymal cysts; calcified lesions need only seizure control.

questions.stem: Which statement about measles and vitamin A is true?

options.text: SSPE is more likely with vitamin A deficiency
Vitamin A treatment reduces measles severity in children in developing countries

questions.explanation: Retinol concentration correlates with severity; vitamin A reduces morbidity and mortality and is recommended for severe measles in the US as well.

questions.stem: Plasma very-long-chain fatty acids are elevated in all of the following peroxisomal disorders except:
questions.explanation: RCDP (PEX7 or plasmalogen synthesis defects) shows elevated phytanic acid and low erythrocyte plasmalogens with normal VLCFA. Zellweger, NALD, and infantile Refsum form the PEX-gene biogenesis spectrum.

questions.stem: A 12-yr-old girl with 2 yr of chronic sinusitis has hemoptysis, respiratory distress, and hematuria. Most helpful test and diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Pulmonary-renal vasculitis that responds to therapy.

questions.stem: Malignant hyperthermia is associated with all except:
questions.explanation: Narcotics are not triggers; succinylcholine and volatile agents are. Succinylcholine also risks hyperkalemia, myoglobinuria, and raised ICP.

questions.stem: Severe life-threatening skin reactions (SJS) are most associated with which anticonvulsant?
questions.explanation: Risk is amplified by rapid titration and co-administration of valproate (inhibits lamotrigine glucuronidation). Phenobarbital and carbamazepine cause hypersensitivity syndrome with hepatitis; HLA-B*15:02 predicts carbamazepine SJS.

questions.stem: A term infant is cyanotic with distress, diminished left breath sounds, scaphoid abdomen, and PMI shifted right. Most important initial intervention?
questions.explanation: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia; decompress bowel occupying the chest and avoid bag-mask ventilation.

questions.stem: Treatment of choice for scabies?
questions.explanation: Lindane is an alternative but potentially neurotoxic; treat household contacts.

questions.stem: A 15-yr-old boy with intellectual disability has macro-orchidism and large prominent ears. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: CGG repeat expansion in FMR1 over 200 (normal 6-54; premutation 55-200) with promoter methylation; the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability. Premutation carriers are at risk for FXTAS and premature ovarian insufficiency.

questions.stem: Infantile spasms, agenesis of the corpus callosum, and chorioretinal lacunae define:
questions.explanation: X-linked dominant, almost exclusively in girls (and XXY males); chorioretinal lacunae are pathognomonic; poor prognosis.

questions.stem: A 12-yr-old girl has 2 days of acute monocular vision loss, 3 yr of vague headaches, a prior brief episode of diplopia, and an episode of foot paresthesias, all separated in time and self-resolving; fundus is normal. Most important diagnostic step?

options.text: MRI of brain and spinal cord

questions.explanation: Retrobulbar optic neuritis with dissemination in time and space suggests multiple sclerosis; MRI shows periventricular and spinal plaques. In children, MOG antibody disease and NMOSD (aquaporin-4) must be distinguished.

questions.stem: The molar tooth sign (thickened, horizontalized superior cerebellar peduncles with vermis hypoplasia) is diagnostic of:
questions.explanation: A ciliopathy (dozens of genes); hypotonia, ataxia, episodic hyperpnea and apnea, oculomotor apraxia, and variable renal, retinal, and hepatic involvement.

questions.stem: A 5-yr-old boy has pelvic girdle weakness, calf pseudohypertrophy, and a Gowers sign. Genetic mechanism?
questions.explanation: Duchenne (X-linked; about two thirds deletions or duplications, the rest point variants); in-frame deletions produce the milder Becker phenotype (reading-frame rule). CK is markedly elevated; steroids, cardiac surveillance, exon-skipping and gene therapies.

questions.stem: A 1,050-g preterm infant has petechiae, microcephaly, thrombocytopenia, and periventricular calcifications on CT. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Periventricular calcifications are characteristic of congenital CMV; toxoplasmosis produces diffuse parenchymal calcifications.

questions.stem: A 4-yr-old blue-eyed girl has malar flush, mild intellectual disability, lens subluxation, iridodonesis, and a tall thin Marfanoid habitus. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency, autosomal recessive; downward lens dislocation (upward in Marfan), thromboembolism, osteoporosis, scoliosis, seizures; cardiomyopathy is not a feature. Short limbs are not part of the phenotype.

questions.stem: A 7-yr-old boy has 3 wk of spiking fevers, chills, chest pain, faint salmon macular rash, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, Hgb 9.7, WBC 26,000, platelets 650,000; echocardiogram shows a pericardial effusion without tamponade. Most likely diagnosis and next step?
questions.explanation: Systemic-onset JRA (now systemic JIA): prolonged fever, evanescent salmon rash, asymptomatic pericarditis, leukocytosis, thrombocytosis, anemia of chronic disease, hepatosplenomegaly; arthritis often develops later. Echocardiogram is the key study because pericardial effusion is the usual cause of the chest pain.

questions.stem: A 5-yr-old has petechiae, fresh bruises, low-grade fever, dizziness, and lethargy; IV placed. Next step?
questions.explanation: Signs of poor CNS perfusion; crystalloid immediately, then rapid antibiotics; steroids only if adrenal insufficiency demonstrated. Multiple organ system failure is the factor that most clearly predicts mortality in shock.

questions.stem: Panayiotopoulos syndrome features prolonged focal autonomic seizures (vomiting, pallor, eye deviation) and which EEG finding?
questions.explanation: Early-onset benign occipital epilepsy; often mistaken for encephalitis or a GI illness.

questions.stem: A 3-mo-old has progressive biphasic stridor, two brief croup episodes, and a 1-cm thigh hemangioma. Airway films most likely show:
questions.explanation: Subglottic hemangioma; beard-distribution facial hemangiomas carry the highest risk, but airway lesions occur without skin lesions. (Propranolol is now first-line.)

questions.stem: Recommended therapy for port-wine stain?
questions.explanation: Flashlamp-pumped pulsed dye laser targets the lesion and spares surrounding tissue. A V1-distribution stain warrants evaluation for Sturge-Weber and glaucoma.

questions.stem: Kearns-Sayre syndrome and Leber hereditary optic neuropathy affect both sexes but are inherited only through the mother. They exemplify:
questions.explanation: mtDNA derives solely from the ovum; all children of an affected mother are at risk, none of an affected father. Heteroplasmy and threshold effect explain variable expression among siblings (MELAS m.3243A>G, MERRF m.8344A>G). Most Kearns-Sayre deletions are sporadic; LHON (m.11778G>A and others) is maternally inherited with incomplete, male-predominant penetrance. Nuclear-encoded mitochondrial disorders (POLG, most complex I subunits) follow Mendelian patterns.

questions.stem: A 19-yr-old has headache, unsteadiness, and 5 yr of worsening hearing; her father had brain surgery and has been deaf since 35. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Bilateral vestibular schwannomas (NF2 gene, merlin, chromosome 22q); meningiomas, ependymomas, and juvenile posterior subcapsular cataracts; cafe-au-lait macules are few or absent. About 10% of NF cases.

questions.stem: Absent septum pellucidum, pituitary hormone deficiencies, and optic nerve hypoplasia characterize:
questions.explanation: Present with nystagmus, poor vision, neonatal hypoglycemia, prolonged jaundice, or micropenis; hypopituitarism (GH, TSH, ACTH, ADH) may evolve, so endocrine surveillance is mandatory. Mostly sporadic; HESX1, SOX2, OTX2 in a minority; associated with young maternal age. A small optic disc with a double-ring sign on fundoscopy is the clue.

questions.stem: An 8-yr-old has 3 days of headache, fever, anorexia, and myalgias, now with a petechial rash prominent on the extremities including palms and soles. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: RMSF rash starts peripherally (wrists and ankles) and spreads centrally; early labs show normal or low WBC with left shift, thrombocytopenia, and hyponatremia.

questions.stem: A 4-mo-old girl has developmental delay, exaggerated startle to sound, macrocephaly, decreased eye contact, and bilateral cherry-red spots. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Tay-Sachs: confirm by leukocyte hexosaminidase A activity. Sandhoff (HEXB) adds hepatosplenomegaly. No disease-modifying therapy; carrier screening and prenatal diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 4-yr-old Middle Eastern boy has brief acute episodes of fever and abdominal pain. Diagnosis and mainstay of treatment?
questions.explanation: Onset usually before age 5; brief self-limited fever with polyserositis at irregular intervals. FMF is autosomal recessive (MEFV).

questions.stem: Based on development, when is the highest risk of self-poisoning?
questions.explanation: Ambulatory, climbing toddlers; child-proof containers rarely deter a motivated toddler.

questions.stem: Periodic lateralized epileptiform discharges in a febrile child with focal seizures and acute cerebral dysfunction are most characteristic of:
questions.explanation: Also seen after acute stroke; PLEDs over the temporal lobe with CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis and red cells should prompt empiric acyclovir.

questions.stem: A 5-yr-old has 3-4 days of fever, headache, abdominal pain, and myalgias after camping in rural Wisconsin, no tick bite recalled, no rash. T 103.4 F, HR 130, RR 40, dehydrated. WBC 2,300 with 65% bands, platelets 57,000, AST 465; smear shows small blue clusters within the cytoplasm of 1% of mononuclear leukocytes. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and transaminase elevation with intracytoplasmic morulae; rash is variable (more common in children with E. chaffeensis than in adults). Doxycycline regardless of age; RMSF and ehrlichiosis are treated identically, so treat on suspicion.

questions.stem: A 3-yr-old boy, normal at birth, has progressive facial coarsening, developmental delay, regurgitant murmur, hepatomegaly, joint stiffness, short stature, hydrocephalus, and no corneal clouding; all affected relatives are boys. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: MPS II (iduronate-2-sulfatase), the only X-linked mucopolysaccharidosis; clear corneas and slower course than MPS I. Dysostosis multiplex, coronary and valvular disease are shared MPS features. Urine GAGs then enzyme assay.

questions.stem: A 3-yr-old girl has fever. Urine is collected by catheterization. What minimum colony count is generally considered diagnostic of UTI?
questions.explanation: 10^3 or greater for catheterized specimens; 10^5 or greater for clean-catch midstream void.

questions.stem: A 14-mo-old girl has irritability, poor walking, genu recurvatum, hypotonia, absent deep tendon reflexes, elevated CSF protein, and slow nerve conduction velocities. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Arylsulfatase A deficiency (ARSA), autosomal recessive; the combination of central white matter disease with a demyelinating peripheral neuropathy (areflexia, slowed NCV, high CSF protein) is the tell; Krabbe shares it. Metachromatic granules in urine sediment and sural nerve. (Presymptomatic HSCT and lentiviral gene therapy now alter outcome.)

questions.stem: A 1-mo-old infant of an HIV-infected mother has indeterminate infection status. Next step?
questions.explanation: All HIV-exposed infants from 6 wk to 12 mo receive Pneumocystis prophylaxis regardless of CD4 count until infection is excluded; after 12 mo, by CD4 count and percentage. (Current: prophylaxis can stop once two negative virologic tests exclude infection.)

questions.stem: A 9-day-old term infant has lethargy, fever, increasing jaundice, hepatomegaly, glucose 10, direct hyperbilirubinemia, AST 700, ALT 650, and blood culture growing a gram-negative rod. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: E. coli sepsis plus hypoglycemia, jaundice, and hepatotoxicity from galactose-1-phosphate is classic; urine reducing substances positive on cow's-milk formula.

questions.stem: A term newborn has mild hepatomegaly, normal head circumference and retinas, urine culture positive for CMV, and normal head ultrasound. The deficit most likely to appear in the next year is:
questions.explanation: Sensorineural hearing loss follows even asymptomatic congenital CMV; CMV is the leading cause of acquired childhood hearing loss in the US. (Current practice: valganciclovir for symptomatic disease with CNS involvement; audiologic surveillance for all.)

questions.stem: Preferred treatment for infant botulism?
questions.explanation: BIG shortens hospital stay; honey is the one avoidable spore source and is unsafe under 1 yr. Antibiotics are avoided (aminoglycosides potentiate blockade; lysis may release toxin). (BabyBIG is now available nationally through the California Department of Public Health.)

questions.stem: In a newborn whose mother was treated for syphilis in pregnancy, all are risk factors for congenital syphilis except:

options.text: Maternal VDRL 1:32 at treatment to 1:16 at delivery
Maternal treatment more than 30 days before delivery

questions.explanation: Risk: nonpenicillin regimen, treatment less than 30 days before delivery, inadequate or undocumented treatment, titers not falling at least fourfold.

questions.stem: A 6-yr-old with meningococcal meningitis develops a swollen left knee on day 5 of antibiotic treatment. Most likely etiology?

options.text: Immune complex deposition from anti-meningococcal antibodies

questions.explanation: Nonsuppurative complications (arthritis, cutaneous vasculitis, pericarditis) appear 4-9 days into the illness, are immune complex-mediated, produce sterile mono- or oligoarticular large-joint effusions, and respond to NSAIDs without sequelae.

quizzes.topicMix: Derm 3, EM 4, Gen 3, ID 10, Metab 7, N-acquired 2, N-cutaneous 3, N-epilepsy 4, N-infection 2, N-malform 2, N-neuromusc 2, Resp 4, Rheum 4

questions.stem: Which is a contraindication to MMR?

options.text: Otitis media with fever of 101 F
Febrile seizure after a prior DTaP

questions.explanation: Measles and mumps vaccines contain negligible egg protein; reactions once attributed to egg were probably gelatin. Pregnancy, severe immunodeficiency, and recent IVIG are the other main contraindications; no association with autism.

questions.stem: A 13-mo-old is found comatose after sleeping late; afebrile, liver 4 cm, glucose 15, bicarbonate 20, ammonia 295, AST 320, ALT 425, normal bilirubin, urine negative for ketones and reducing substances. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Nonketotic hypoglycemia with or without hyperammonemia at this age; Reye-like presentation, and some cases are first labeled SIDS. Acylcarnitine profile (C8) is diagnostic.

questions.stem: A 12-yr-old girl has 6 mo of knee and elbow arthralgia, swollen hands, intermittent fever, 15-lb weight loss, ITP 3 yr earlier, a severe sunburn one summer, mouth sores 2 yr ago, Hct 25%, positive Coombs, and hematuria. Diagnosis and treatment?
questions.explanation: Arthritis, oral ulcers, photosensitivity, thrombocytopenia, hemolytic anemia, hematuria; manifestations need not be simultaneous. With positive dsDNA and undetectable complement, prednisone is treatment of choice for exacerbation.

questions.stem: A 2-wk-old has episodes of cyanosis and bradycardia triggered by crying after esophageal atresia repair; when calm, mild retractions, rhonchi, prolonged expiration. Cause?
questions.explanation: Very common after EA/TEF repair; also the usual cause of chronic barking cough and wheeze in these children years later.

questions.stem: A 9-mo-old is limp, unresponsive, pulse 35, occasional gasps. After CPR and intubation, IV attempts fail. Next step?

options.text: Intraosseous needle with fluids and inotropes

questions.explanation: IO within 1-2 min of failed access; anterior tibia; labs, culture, fluids, and drugs all go through it.

questions.stem: A 13-mo-old has 2 days of fever, lethargy, and irritability, then left arm and face twitching and left weakness; CSF 70 WBC (85% lymphocytes), 400 RBC, protein 140, glucose 80, Gram stain negative; MRI shows right temporal abnormality. Study most likely to identify a treatable illness promptly, and empiric therapy?

options.text: CSF bacterial culture; nafcillin, cefotaxime, metronidazole
Maternal and infant titers; antituberculous therapy

questions.explanation: Focal seizure, focal deficit, hemorrhagic lymphocytic CSF, and temporal lobe lesion are HSV encephalitis until proven otherwise; CSF PCR is 90-95% sensitive and acyclovir must not wait for the result.

questions.stem: A 2-yr-old has symmetric psoriasiform lesions in perioral, acral, and perineal distribution and on cheeks, knees, and elbows, with mild alopecia and chronic diarrhea. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Zinc malabsorption (SLC39A4); treat with oral zinc. Biotinidase deficiency and CF produce similar rashes and belong in the differential.

questions.stem: A 4-yr-old girl has severe failure to thrive (18 lb, 30 inches), high-pitched voice, sclerodermatous skin over the abdomen, near-total alopecia, small jaw and face relative to head circumference, and normal mental and motor development. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Rapidly progressive aging phenotype with normal cognition; de novo dominant LMNA c.1824C>T producing progerin (a laminopathy, identified 2003 after the source's "unknown etiology"). Death from coronary and cerebrovascular disease in the teens; lonafarnib (farnesyltransferase inhibitor) modestly extends survival.

questions.stem: A 5-yr-old girl with severe intellectual disability, microcephaly, hand-wringing stereotypies, poor growth, and seizures has a MECP2 mutation. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Normal early development, then regression at 6-18 mo with loss of purposeful hand use and language, deceleration of head growth, stereotypies, breathing dysregulation, and autistic features; X-linked dominant, mostly de novo, almost all in girls. (Trofinetide approved 2023; CDKL5 and FOXG1 are the main phenocopies.)

questions.stem: Displacement of medulla, fourth ventricle, and cerebellar vermis through the foramen magnum in a child with myelomeningocele is:
questions.explanation: Chiari I is isolated tonsillar descent (syrinx, headache, later presentation); Dandy-Walker is cystic fourth ventricle with vermian agenesis and high tentorium, not tonsillar descent.

questions.stem: A 5-yr-old girl is evaluated for progressive walking difficulty that worsens through the day and is much better after sleep; afternoon exam shows leg rigidity and dystonic foot posturing. This disorder responds dramatically to:
questions.explanation: Dopa-responsive dystonia (Segawa; GCH1, autosomal dominant with reduced penetrance, female predominance); diurnal fluctuation, often misdiagnosed as diplegic CP. Small doses of levodopa are curative; also consider in any childhood dystonia with parkinsonism.

questions.stem: An 11-yr-old wrestled with another boy, sustaining facial and neck bruises, and awoke the next morning with dysarthria and right-sided weakness, arm greater than leg. Most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Minor neck trauma, torsion, or hyperextension (roller coasters, chiropractic manipulation, the hairdresser's sink) precede many childhood dissections; MRA or CTA of the neck; most recover without deficit.

questions.stem: A 7-mo-old with up-to-date immunizations has gradual fever, lethargy, and irritability; CSF has 1,500 WBC (84% granulocytes), glucose 12, protein 70, Gram stain negative. Most likely agent?
questions.explanation: Meningococcus and pneumococcus are the leading causes of non-neonatal bacterial meningitis; Hib vaccine has nearly eliminated Hib. Empiric vancomycin plus ceftriaxone (or cefotaxime) covers resistant pneumococci.

questions.stem: A 5-yr-old has a tender 3-cm left axillary node for 3 wk, unchanged after a course of cephalexin; low-grade fever and fatigue have resolved. The family has cats, and healing scratches are present on both arms. Most reasonable approach?
questions.explanation: Cat-scratch disease (Bartonella henselae) resolves spontaneously over weeks to months; no antibiotic is clearly beneficial in uncomplicated disease (azithromycin modestly hastens node regression). Needle aspiration for pain; avoid incision and drainage. Parinaud oculoglandular syndrome, hepatosplenic disease, and encephalopathy are the atypical forms.

questions.stem: A woman with classic PKU reaches adulthood and becomes pregnant with a poorly controlled diet. Fetal risks include all except:
questions.explanation: Maternal PKU embryopathy: microcephaly, CHD, growth restriction, developmental delay; the baby is an obligate carrier.

questions.stem: An 11-mo-old is treated for Kawasaki disease with IVIG 2 g/kg. First MMR should be given at:
questions.explanation: Live vaccines are deferred at least 11 mo after high-dose IVIG because passive antibody impairs replication and immunogenicity.

questions.stem: A 4-yr-old has sudden sore throat, fever, dysphagia, labored breathing, drooling, tripod posture. Next step?

options.text: Direct laryngoscopy in the operating room

questions.explanation: Epiglottitis requires immediate controlled airway protection.

questions.stem: SVT is characterized by all except:
questions.explanation: Abrupt onset and offset. Verapamil can cause cardiac arrest in infants; adenosine is the drug of choice, synchronized cardioversion if unstable.

questions.stem: EEG pattern of early infantile epileptic encephalopathy (Ohtahara)?
questions.explanation: Tonic spasms with burst suppression in the first weeks; structural and genetic (STXBP1, KCNQ2) causes; often evolves into West syndrome.

questions.stem: A child has multiple discrete skin-colored 1- to 3-mm dome-shaped smooth papules on the face with central umbilication. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Poxvirus; a plug of cheesy material can be expressed; face, eyelids, neck, axillae, thighs.

questions.stem: Uniparental disomy:

options.text: Can lead to autosomal recessive disorders
Is associated with advanced maternal age

questions.explanation: Both homologs from one parent, usually by trisomy rescue; isodisomy exposes recessive alleles, and heterodisomy or isodisomy of an imprinted region produces Prader-Willi (maternal UPD 15) or Angelman (paternal UPD 15).

questions.stem: Incontinentia pigmenti is associated with all except:

options.text: Linear vesicles and erythematous streaks along Blaschko lines

questions.explanation: X-linked dominant (IKBKG/NEMO), lethal in males; the rash evolves vesicular to verrucous to hyperpigmented to atrophic; neonatal seizures and retinal neovascularization.

questions.stem: A 2-yr-old with spastic diplegic cerebral palsy. Brain MRI is most likely to show:
questions.explanation: PVL affects the periventricular white matter carrying the leg fibers of the corticospinal tract; extensive cystic PVL in the neonatal period is a strong predictor of CP. Basal ganglia and thalamic injury underlie dyskinetic CP after term asphyxia or kernicterus.

questions.stem: The Gowers sign demonstrates:
questions.explanation: The child climbs up the legs to stand; classic in Duchenne but nonspecific for proximal weakness (SMA, myopathies, dermatomyositis).

questions.stem: A 12-yr-old with intermittent right-sided headaches has severe headache, a generalized seizure, sudden collapse into flaccid coma, and nuchal rigidity without fever. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: AVM is the leading cause of spontaneous intracranial hemorrhage in children; subarachnoid blood gives meningismus; CT then angiography.

questions.stem: Greatest risk of meningitis after documented occult bacteremia is associated with:
questions.explanation: A positive blood culture for meningococcus is almost always accompanied by focal disease; the child must be recalled and treated immediately.

questions.stem: All statements about neonatal HSV are true except:

options.text: Primary maternal infection transmits more often than recurrent
Most cases are acquired at delivery rather than in utero
Most mothers of affected newborns have a history of genital HSV
Most mothers are asymptomatic at delivery

questions.explanation: Only 15-20% of mothers have a history and about 25% have relevant symptoms at delivery, which is why absence of maternal history is not reassuring.

questions.stem: A 15-yr-old Ashkenazi Jewish girl has chronic fatigue, pallor, spleen to the iliac fossa, normal cognition, Hgb 9.0, WBC 3,000, platelets 60,000. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Glucocerebrosidase (GBA1) deficiency; massive splenomegaly, cytopenias, bone pain with Erlenmeyer flask deformity, and no CNS involvement in type I. Niemann-Pick A also gives massive spleen but with neurodegeneration. Enzyme replacement (or substrate reduction) is effective for visceral and hematologic disease.

questions.stem: A 13-yr-old boy has 4 wk of chronic cough, fever, fatigue, weight loss, prominent axillary and epitrochlear nodes, hilar adenopathy, and noncaseating granulomas on node biopsy. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Elevated ESR, hyperproteinemia, hypercalcemia, hypercalciuria, eosinophilia, elevated ACE are common; biopsy is definitive. Yearly slit-lamp exam monitors for irreversible ocular damage.

questions.stem: A 2-yr-old with croup at 3 AM has barky cough, stridor only with crying, SpO2 96%, drinking well, consolable. Next step?

options.text: Nasal wash for influenza and RSV

questions.explanation: Stridor at rest would add racemic epinephrine. Parainfluenza is the usual agent; steeple sign on film.

questions.stem: A 12-yr-old with spina bifida (shunt, multiple surgeries, chronic catheterization, ampicillin prophylaxis) develops respiratory distress during anesthetic induction. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Urticaria, wheeze, hypotension; multiple surgeries and catheterization are the risk factors; bananas, kiwi, and avocado cross-react.

questions.stem: An 18-mo-old has clusters of spasms on awakening and hypsarrhythmia. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Hypsarrhythmia: high-voltage chaotic slowing with multifocal spikes. ACTH or high-dose prednisolone, or vigabatrin (first-line in TSC). Etiology (TSC, structural, metabolic, genetic) drives prognosis.

questions.stem: Nevus sebaceus (Jadassohn) is associated with all except:

options.text: Yellow-orange plaque on scalp or face

questions.explanation: Benign-appearing plaques that can give rise to secondary tumors (basal cell carcinoma, trichoblastoma); the source recommends excision before adulthood.

questions.stem: A 1-yr-old has a classic autosomal recessive disease (such as CF). The father is tested and, with 99% confidence, is not a carrier. Most likely explanation?

options.text: Mutation to an autosomal dominant trait
Imprinting of the missing recessive gene

questions.explanation: Two copies of the maternal mutant chromosome; nonpaternity is the pragmatic alternative to raise gently.

questions.stem: Genetic testing shows a de novo deletion of 15q11-q13 on the maternally derived chromosome 15. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Loss of maternal UBE3A expression (deletion, paternal UPD, imprinting defect, or UBE3A mutation): happy demeanor, ataxic gait, absent speech, microcephaly, and epilepsy with a characteristic high-amplitude slow EEG. Prader-Willi is loss of the paternal contribution.

questions.stem: A 10-mo-old infant from an urban area presents with T 39.3 C and an unremarkable exam. Which is a risk factor for occult bacteremia?

options.text: Absence of pneumonia signs on exam

questions.explanation: Socioeconomic status, race, gender, and age do not appear to affect risk among children 3-36 mo. (Dated: post-PCV occult bacteremia rates are far lower than in the source era.)

questions.stem: Fabry disease is characterized by all except:
questions.explanation: X-linked alpha-galactosidase A deficiency; painful neuropathic crises, angiokeratomas, cornea verticillata, hypohidrosis, renal failure, and stroke in young adults; cognition is spared. ERT and migalastat are available.

questions.stem: A newborn has congenital heart block. Most likely etiology?
questions.explanation: Transplacental IgG, usually anti-Ro, between 12 and 16 wk; block is permanent and often needs pacing.

questions.stem: A 7-yr-old with trisomy 21 whose VSD closed spontaneously now has pulmonary hypertension with normal intracardiac anatomy, SpO2 98%, and is sleepy and irritable with mouth breathing and 3+ tonsils. Next step?

options.text: Diagnostic studies for obstructive sleep apnea

questions.explanation: Trisomy 21 carries high OSA risk; the pulmonary hypertension is from nocturnal hypoxia and hypercarbia, not the heart.

questions.stem: To confirm endotracheal tube placement, all of the following except:
questions.explanation: AP film is standard; ETCO2 is the most accurate in a perfusing rhythm, less so in asystole.

questions.stem: Rasmussen encephalitis is characterized by all except:
questions.explanation: Progressive unihemispheric atrophy with hemiparesis, hemianopia, and aphasia; hemispherectomy is the definitive treatment of the epilepsy.

questions.stem: Which contacts should receive rifampin after invasive N. meningitidis in a child?

options.text: Unimmunized children in the same household and daycare
All children and adults in the same household or daycare regardless of immunization status
All household members if an unimmunized child under 48 mo is present

questions.explanation: All household, daycare, and nursery contacts; the index patient also needs rifampin if treated with penicillin (does not clear carriage). Rifampin, ceftriaxone, or ciprofloxacin are acceptable.

questions.stem: A 17-yr-old has recurrent exercise intolerance with muscle cramps and is otherwise well. Most likely to develop during episodes?
questions.explanation: Muscle glycogenosis (McArdle, myophosphorylase; PYGM): second-wind phenomenon, flat lactate on ischemic forearm test, rhabdomyolysis with risk of renal failure.

questions.stem: Most likely cause of fungal pneumonia in immunocompetent persons in the Ohio and Mississippi river valleys?
questions.explanation: Blastomyces shares the region but is less common outside the northern Midwest; Coccidioides is the arid Southwest.

questions.stem: A 3-day-old 4.5-kg infant of a nondiabetic mother is hypotonic and poorly responsive with glucose 22 mg/dL and receives a 2 mL/kg D10W minibolus; she improves, then seizes 3 hr later with glucose 18. Most appropriate next step?

options.text: Minibolus of D10W plus continuous IV glucose infusion

questions.explanation: A bolus without a maintenance infusion (start 4-8 mg/kg/min) guarantees recurrence; escalating glucose requirements above about 10-12 mg/kg/min define hyperinsulinism. Magnesium is not part of the immediate evaluation of a hypotonic hypoglycemic neonate (hypomagnesemia presents with irritability and hyperreflexia); glucose, electrolytes, blood gas, and culture are.

questions.stem: Which is recognized to be associated with infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis?

options.text: Any macrolide in pregnancy or in the first 2 wk of life
Any macrolide in the first 2 wk of life
Erythromycin given in the first 2 wk of life

questions.explanation: A 7- to 10-fold relative risk of IHPS in infants under 6 wk treated with oral erythromycin, highest in the first 2 wk of life and with courses of 14 days or more.

questions.stem: A 14-mo-old white boy has 2 mo of chorea after failure to thrive and emesis from 4 mo, hyperreflexia, erosions of lips and fingers, normal ammonia, and elevated uric acid; an older brother is institutionalized. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Complete HPRT1 deficiency, X-linked; dystonia and chorea, self-injury, uric acid nephropathy. Allopurinol controls urate but not the neurologic phenotype; partial deficiency gives gout without neurologic disease.

questions.stem: Which contacts should receive rifampin after invasive Hib disease in a child?

options.text: All household members if the group includes an unimmunized or partially immunized child under 48 mo
All household or daycare contacts regardless of immunization
Unimmunized children under 48 mo in household and daycare

questions.explanation: Contrast with meningococcus : Hib prophylaxis is triggered by the presence of a susceptible young child, and then covers the whole contact group including the index patient.

questions.stem: All are features of scarlet fever except:
questions.explanation: Sandpaper rash, Pastia lines in creases, white then red strawberry tongue, desquamation toward the end of week 1.

questions.stem: A 4-wk-old has gagging and gasping episodes, mild cough, rhinorrhea, afebrile, clear lungs, WBC 42,000 with 87% lymphocytes. Agent?
questions.explanation: Lymphocyte-predominant leukocytosis in an afebrile infant with gasping episodes is characteristic of pertussis.

quizzes.topicMix: Derm 4, EM 3, Gen 2, ID 10, Metab 8, N-acquired 2, N-cutaneous 3, N-epilepsy 4, N-infection 2, N-malform 2, N-neuromusc 2, Resp 4, Rheum 4

questions.stem: A 1-mo-old develops bloody diarrhea with fever. Most likely agent?
questions.explanation: Salmonella is by far the most common cause of febrile gastroenteritis in early infancy; Campylobacter is second. Shigella is rare in infancy and common at 1-3 yr; rotavirus rarely causes bloody stool.

questions.stem: A 10-day-old has profound coma after an illness with emesis and hypotonia; 4+ ketonuria, pH 6.9, PCO2 19, anion gap 37, ANC 400. Diagnosis, and additional therapy?
questions.explanation: Organic acidemia: ketoacidosis with anion gap, hyperammonemia, neutropenia. Some MMA is cobalamin-responsive (1-2 mg/day hydroxocobalamin); carnitine and protein restriction otherwise. Propionic acidemia is the mimic. On newborn screen (C3 acylcarnitine).

questions.stem: A 9-yr-old girl has 1 mo of difficulty combing hair and climbing stairs, a positive Gowers sign, and a faint maculopapular rash over the MCP joints. Most appropriate study, and diagnosis?
questions.explanation: CK was 7,500 IU/mL. JDM classically affects preadolescent girls with insidious proximal weakness and vasculitic rash over knuckles, malar area, or eyelids. Dysphagia and drooling later reflect palatopharyngeal striated muscle weakness.

questions.stem: A 5-mo-old after 3 days of cough has RR 80, marked retractions, diminished breath sounds, diffuse crackles, no stridor, SpO2 80% on 100% nonrebreather, pallor, weak pulses. Immediate action?
questions.explanation: Persistent hypoxia on 100% FiO2 is respiratory failure.

questions.stem: A 15-yr-old started carbamazepine 4 wk ago and now has diffuse erythematous macular rash, fever, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, and elevated transaminases. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Onset 1-3 mo after starting aromatic anticonvulsants; hepatitis and lymphadenopathy are uncommon in SJS or TEN. Cross-reactivity among phenytoin, carbamazepine, and phenobarbital. (HLA-B*15:02 screening in Asian populations for carbamazepine.)

questions.stem: An adolescent has early-morning myoclonic jerks and generalized polyspike-wave discharges. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: 4-6 Hz polyspike-wave, often photosensitive; valproate or levetiracetam; lifelong treatment is usual and carbamazepine can aggravate.

questions.stem: A 3-yr-old after a two-story fall is alert, pulse 190, BP 70/30, femur fracture, diffusely tender abdomen; after 20 mL/kg Ringer, pulse 180, BP 72/35. Next step?
questions.explanation: Repeated early crystalloid boluses; transfuse as blood loss becomes evident. Abdominal CT with IV contrast is the standard study in stable blunt trauma.

questions.stem: A 6-yr-old with NF1 has an optic glioma confined to the right optic nerve on routine MRI, with normal neurologic, retinal, and visual exams (20/20 bilaterally). Correct management?

options.text: Radiation to the right optic nerve

questions.explanation: NF1-associated optic pathway gliomas (pilocytic, about 15% of patients) are usually indolent; treatment (carboplatin-vincristine, or selumetinib) is reserved for visual decline or progression, and radiation is avoided because of secondary malignancy and moyamoya risk.

questions.stem: A baby is born with classic features of Down syndrome. Indications for chromosome studies include:

options.text: All of the above; studies are indicated in every affected child

questions.explanation: A karyotype distinguishes nondisjunction (recurrence about 1%) from a translocation; if translocation, both parents are studied, and a carrier parent raises sibling recurrence to about 10-15% (higher for maternal carriers, 100% for a 21;21 carrier).

questions.stem: Causes of megalencephaly include all except:
questions.explanation: Congenital CMV causes microcephaly. Marrow expansion, storage disease and leukodystrophy (Canavan, Alexander, Tay-Sachs, GA1), CSF excess, subdural collections, and benign familial macrocephaly enlarge the head.

questions.stem: A floppy infant who never sat has tongue fasciculations and areflexia. Diagnosis and gene?
questions.explanation: Homozygous SMN1 deletion (about 95%); SMN2 copy number modifies severity. Alert face, bell-shaped chest, paradoxical breathing. Nusinersen, risdiplam, and onasemnogene make newborn screening and presymptomatic treatment the standard.

questions.stem: A 5-yr-old with 6 wk of morning headaches with vomiting, now irritable and moody. Most likely exam finding?
questions.explanation: Posterior fossa tumor with raised ICP; papilledema takes time to develop and must be sought in every child with headache. Acutely, visual acuity is preserved in papilledema, unlike papillitis of optic neuritis.

questions.stem: Most common cause of viral meningoencephalitis?
questions.explanation: Summer and fall; CSF PCR has replaced culture. Late-summer encephalitis after freshwater or saltwater marsh exposure in the Northeast raises eastern equine encephalitis; HSV is the treatable cause not to miss.

questions.stem: Recommended agent for RMSF in a child under 8?
questions.explanation: Doxycycline is preferred at any age; chloramphenicol carries higher mortality, and dental staining is unlikely with a single doxycycline course.

questions.stem: A previously healthy 2-wk-old has progressive lethargy, rigidity, opisthotonos alternating with flaccidity, hypoglycemia, metabolic acidosis, cerebral edema, and elevated leucine, isoleucine, and valine. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase deficiency; leucine is the neurotoxic amino acid. Crisis management is dialysis or hemofiltration plus reversal of catabolism; on newborn screen.

questions.stem: Low complement may be associated with all of the following except:
questions.explanation: Complement is normal in nephrotic syndrome; immune complex diseases reduce CH50.

questions.stem: A disk battery is seen in a child's nose. Most important management consideration?

options.text: It may leak and cause local tissue damage

questions.explanation: Chemical burn or pressure necrosis; immediate removal, avoiding pushing it posteriorly.

questions.stem: An 8-yr-old girl has large cafe-au-lait spots with irregular borders, precocious puberty, and polyostotic fibrous dysplasia. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Postzygotic activating GNAS mutation; irregular "coast of Maine" borders contrast with the smooth "coast of California" macules of NF1; hyperfunctioning endocrinopathies.

questions.stem: A 3-yr-old lost consciousness for 5 min at home; you see him an hour later. Most helpful in distinguishing seizure from syncope?
questions.explanation: Syncope produces loss of tone and rapid recovery once supine, though a few convulsive jerks may occur; a prolonged postictal state points to seizure.

questions.stem: Which pool safety measure would most likely have prevented a 2-yr-old's drowning?

options.text: 5-ft ornamental iron isolation fence (vertical bars 3 inches apart)

questions.explanation: Fencing that cannot be climbed; children under 3-4 cannot swim safely; covers are dangerous.

questions.stem: PHACE(S) syndrome is associated with all except:
questions.explanation: P is posterior fossa (Dandy-Walker, cerebellar hypoplasia). Cerebrovascular anomalies are the major source of morbidity and shape the safety of propranolol.

questions.stem: Risk of an autosomal recessive disease in the offspring of a first-cousin mating?
questions.explanation: Roughly twice the background risk for an autosomal recessive trait in nonconsanguineous matings (first cousins share 1/8 of their genes; coefficient of inbreeding 1/16).

questions.stem: An 18-mo-old has pendular nystagmus, head nodding, and torticollis with a normal MRI. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Self-limited once imaging excludes a chiasmatic or hypothalamic glioma.

questions.stem: A child has frequent falls, pes cavus, hammer toes, peroneal atrophy, absent stretch reflexes, and uniformly slowed NCVs. Most likely mutation?
questions.explanation: CMT1A, 17p12 duplication, autosomal dominant; onion bulbs on nerve biopsy. Deletion of the same segment causes hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies.

questions.stem: Which therapy has shown long-term benefit in some patients with X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy?
questions.explanation: Only before substantial cerebral involvement (low Loes score, minimal symptoms), which is the rationale for newborn screening and serial MRI in presymptomatic boys. Lorenzo's oil normalizes VLCFA but does not arrest cerebral disease.

questions.stem: An 8-yr-old presents in late summer with acute meningoencephalitis after swimming in a stagnant pond. Etiology?
questions.explanation: Primary amebic meningoencephalitis via the cribriform plate; purulent CSF with motile trophozoites on wet mount; nearly always fatal despite amphotericin and miltefosine.

questions.stem: Which pregnant woman should receive intrapartum GBS prophylaxis?

options.text: GBS-positive at 37 wk, planned cesarean without rupture of membranes
GBS-negative at 37 wk, rupture of membranes over 20 hr at 39 wk
GBS-negative at 35 wk, spontaneous labor at 36 wk
GBS status unknown, previous infant with invasive GBS disease

questions.explanation: Indications: positive prenatal screen, GBS bacteriuria in pregnancy, or a previous infant with invasive GBS disease; unknown status with risk factors (preterm, ROM 18 hr or more, intrapartum fever). Prelabor cesarean with intact membranes does not require prophylaxis.

questions.stem: A blonde, blue-eyed girl admitted at 2.5 mo to rule out pyloric stenosis has poor development, eczema, and a musty odor. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency; the odor is phenylacetate. Children appear normal at birth and are identified by newborn screening; overtreatment causes anorexia, lethargy, rash, and diarrhea from phenylalanine deficiency.

questions.stem: Most common cause of death from Kawasaki disease in the early phase?
questions.explanation: Before aneurysms form, severe myocarditis can cause cardiogenic shock. Splenic rupture is not a feature; arthritis, aseptic meningitis, urethritis, and gallbladder hydrops are.

questions.stem: A healthy 4-wk-old has stridor since birth with suprasternal and subcostal retractions, feeds well, spits up frequently. Cause?
questions.explanation: Worse with URIs and supine; self-limited.

questions.stem: A 2-day-old well-appearing term neonate has multiple firm yellow-white 1- to 2-mm papules and pustules with an erythematous flare on the trunk; Wright stain shows eosinophils. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Benign, self-limited, in about 50% of term infants; peaks day 2; spares palms and soles. Transient neonatal pustular melanosis shows neutrophils and leaves hyperpigmented macules.

questions.stem: Childhood absence epilepsy EEG?
questions.explanation: Provoked by hyperventilation; ethosuximide first-line. Slow spike-wave is Lennox-Gastaut. Hyperventilation-induced 3 Hz slowing without spikes is a normal finding in children.

questions.stem: All of the following may be complications of influenza except:
questions.explanation: Otitis and viral or bacterial (S. aureus, pneumococcus) pneumonia are common; benign acute childhood myositis (calf pain, elevated CK) follows influenza B. Reye syndrome follows salicylate use during influenza or varicella, which is why aspirin is avoided in febrile children.

questions.stem: An infant has macrocephaly, widened Sylvian fissures, high T2 signal in the basal ganglia, and catastrophic deterioration during an intercurrent infection. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: GCDH deficiency; striatal necrosis during catabolic crisis leaves a dystonic-dyskinetic movement disorder; subdural hematomas and retinal hemorrhages can mimic abusive head trauma (as can Menkes disease and osteogenesis imperfecta). On newborn screen (C5DC); lysine-restricted diet, carnitine, and aggressive sick-day management prevent crises.

questions.stem: A 20-mo-old develops hemolytic anemia, anuria, azotemia, and thrombocytopenia after febrile bloody diarrhea. Most likely agent?
questions.explanation: Shiga toxin-producing E. coli O157:H7 causes most HUS; S. dysenteriae serotype 1 is occasionally responsible.

questions.stem: A 3-day-old 4.5-kg infant of a nondiabetic mother is hypoglycemic; after a D10W bolus and continuous infusion she needs 25% dextrose centrally to hold glucose at 45 mg/dL. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Persistent hyperinsulinism (formerly nesidioblastosis); K-ATP channel defects (ABCC8, KCNJ11) are the most common, familial or sporadic. Diazoxide or octreotide; some need near-total pancreatectomy (diffuse) or focal resection. Symptomatic neonatal hypoglycemia gets a 2 mL/kg D10W minibolus followed by infusion.

questions.stem: All are SLE diagnostic criteria except:
questions.explanation: Diagnosis requires 4 of 11 criteria (1997 ACR; since revised by SLICC 2012 and EULAR/ACR 2019).

questions.stem: Strongest risk factor for SIDS among the following?
questions.explanation: Postnatal exposure also matters, but prenatal maternal smoking dominates. Prematurity, low birth weight, prone position, and African-American heritage are associated; immunizations are not. Long QT and MCAD are rare associations to suspect when SIDS recurs in a family.

questions.stem: Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon (thrombocytopenia, microangiopathic hemolysis, consumptive coagulopathy) is seen most often with:
questions.explanation: Not a complication of ordinary infantile hemangioma.

questions.stem: Seizures in BECTS (self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes) typically occur during:
questions.explanation: About 70% in sleep; hemifacial sensorimotor seizures with drooling and speech arrest; centrotemporal spikes activated by sleep; remits by adolescence.

questions.stem: A 3-yr-old whose mother was just diagnosed with TB has a positive PPD and a nonspecific RLL infiltrate. Best way to confirm the diagnosis?

options.text: Three consecutive early-morning gastric aspirates for culture

questions.explanation: Yield about 50%; bronchoscopy is lower. Negative cultures never exclude TB, and the child is treated on epidemiologic grounds.

questions.stem: A 2-day-old boy has poor feeding, vomiting, lethargy progressing to coma, respiratory alkalosis, hyperammonemia, and elevated urine orotic acid. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: X-linked; most common urea cycle defect. Orotic aciduria distinguishes OTC from CPS1 and NAGS deficiency (low orotate); respiratory alkalosis without acidosis distinguishes urea cycle defects from organic acidemias. Heterozygous females can present later with Reye-like episodes.

questions.stem: A 9-yr-old has a positive PPD on routine screening, no symptoms, normal exam and chest film. Best interpretation?

options.text: Recent exposure but neither infection nor disease

questions.explanation: Reactive skin test without clinical or radiographic disease defines infection; 5-10% of untreated infected persons progress to disease. Treat with isoniazid 9 mo (or current rifampin-based short regimens).

questions.stem: A 3-mo-old has a generalized seizure, marked hepatomegaly to the umbilicus, glucose 25, CO2 12, uric acid 7.1, cholesterol 270, triglycerides 550. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency (von Gierke): fasting hypoglycemia with lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, hyperlipidemia, and doll facies; no glycemic response to glucagon. Oral fructose (and galactose) will not raise glucose because hepatic release of free glucose requires the deficient enzyme; uncooked cornstarch does.

questions.stem: A child suffers a provoked bite from a stray dog that animal control captured; the dog appears healthy. Most appropriate action?

options.text: Confine and observe the dog for 10 days for signs of rabies
No prophylaxis needed because the attack was provoked
Submit the dog's head for rabies examination

questions.explanation: Healthy dogs, cats, and ferrets are held for 10-day observation; prophylaxis begins at the first sign of rabies in the animal, which is then euthanized and tested.

questions.stem: A 7-yr-old "A" student develops progressive hyperactivity labeled ADHD, then deteriorating school performance, difficulty understanding speech on the telephone, and seizures 6 mo later; exam shows diffuse hyperpigmentation, spasticity, and reduced reflexes. Diagnosis and best test?
questions.explanation: ABCD1 defect; parieto-occipital demyelination with contrast-enhancing edge, central auditory processing loss, adrenal insufficiency (hyperpigmentation; check ACTH stimulation). VLCFA may be normal in some heterozygous females, so carrier testing requires mutation analysis. HSCT before symptoms (Loes score) or elivaldogene gene therapy halts cerebral disease; on newborn screen in many states.

questions.stem: Which serologic pattern is most consistent with successful treatment of primary syphilis 2 yr earlier?
questions.explanation: Nontreponemal tests (VDRL, RPR) are quantifiable and usually revert within 1 yr of adequate treatment of primary syphilis; treponemal tests (MHA-TP, FTA-ABS) usually stay positive for life.

questions.stem: A previously healthy 6-mo-old develops hepatomegaly, lethargy, jaundice, severe emesis, and dehydration with positive urine reducing substances; fruit juices and baby food were added at 5 mo. Diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Aldolase B deficiency; asymptomatic until sucrose or fructose exposure; older children learn to avoid sweets. Fructose and sucrose elimination is curative.

questions.stem: All are characteristic of congenital rubella syndrome except:
questions.explanation: Snuffles is congenital syphilis.

questions.stem: A 15-yr-old on IV ampicillin for pneumonia develops bloody diarrhea on hospital day 6; she is otherwise improved. Most appropriate action?
questions.explanation: The first step in C. difficile-associated diarrhea is stopping the inciting antibiotic; toxins A and B mediate disease. (Current: oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin for confirmed disease.)
